textHeavy: Lines 15-26 (about 400 words of prose after the frontmatter): Quick Take and 'You will be able to'. Defines new, this and super, names the three constructor bugs (a missing super.new silently passes defaults, addr = addr, a virtual call from a parent constructor), gives the building-floors analogy and where it breaks, and lists four objectives. Nothing visual appears until <BeforeYouStart /> at line 27.

Lines 31-42 (about 255 words, just under the threshold): 'Why objects need constructors' (vocabulary recap of class, object, handle, property, method and initializer; Packet p; is null until new; what the constructor is for; Table 6-7 defaults) and the opening of 'What new does' (no return type, the left-hand side decides the class, default and by-name arguments). The first code is at line 43.

Lines 75-93 (about 350 words): the four constructor rules (implicit constructor, no timing control, local/protected but never static/virtual, shallow copy skips new), then the three-step construction order, 'undefined until initialized' and the C/D predict prompt. This is the page's core mental model, and it is carried by two lists. Its only picture is the trace table hidden in the collapsed <details> at line 116.

Lines 165-172 (about 195 words, dense): the 'Read the diagram this way' paragraph. It is the only place in Build Your Mental Model that explains the virtual-call-on-a-half-built-object pitfall (objective 4), and it does so in words only. It runs straight into the start of the 'this' section.

Lines 191-207 (about 295 words): where this is legal (non-static methods, constraints, covergroups, type(this); no this in a static method), this being optional when nothing clashes, this and null handles (tool-dependent behaviour), the 'this needs no separate diagram' remark, what overriding means, and the two uses of super.

Lines 260-272 (about 235 words): the remaining chaining rules (an implicit constructor follows the same rule, super reaches one level only, an extends Base(args) clause forbids an explicit super.new), then the definitions of global and instance constants, before the frame_item code.

Lines 316-336 (about 420 words, including the Recap bullets and the Make It Work intro): real-testbench practice (identity at birth from a static counter plus a const id; passing cfg or vif into new; short constructors with no waiting, no virtual calls and randomization after new; the UVM fixed constructor shapes and build_phase), the five-bullet Recap with no recap visual, and the intro to the three-level example.

Lines 403-443 (about 675 words, the longest stretch on the page): 'Why the log has this shape', 'Run it', the six-step 'How to write a constructor chain', the checklist, the four Push Further initialization-order corner cases (super.new arguments evaluated before initializers, 'undefined' vs a tool printing 0, virtual dispatch from a constructor compared with C++ and Java, a static counter vs a shallow copy) and the qualifier/singleton intro, up to the tb_registry snippet at line 444.

Lines 494-507 (about 275 words): the typed-constructor-call bullets, then 'Why UVM constructors have fixed signatures' (m_uvm_object_create_func's create(), the component registry's create_component, the uvm_object and uvm_component constructor signatures, a component with no constructor failing to compile, extra arguments needing defaults). These are call chains, described only in prose.
Not flagged: lines 726-749 are References (citations, not teaching prose).

additions.where: Quick Take, after 'The Analogy' bullet (line 19) and before 'You will be able to' (line 21)
additions.what: A compact anchor picture, 'build from the root up', as an inline <svg viewBox="0 0 360 220" role="img" aria-label="..." style={{width:'100%',maxWidth:360}}> inside <figure> with a <figcaption>. Use marker ids prefixed 'ctor-' and theme-safe colours (currentColor, mid-tone cyan and amber). Draw three stacked floors with the root at the bottom: base_item (root base class), bus_item, crc_item. Each floor has two numbered cells: 'initializers' (fixtures) and 'rest of body' (finishing work). Number them 1-6 from the bottom up. A dashed arrow on the left points down: 'super.new calls go down first'. A solid arrow on the right points up: 'work comes back up, root first'. An amber flag on cell 2 (base_item body) reads 'if a virtual method were called here, crc_item's override would run while addr and crc are undefined (§8.17 NOTE 2)'. Caption: 'Conceptual illustration of §8.7 and §8.17 for the classes you build in Make It Work (crc_item extends bus_item extends base_item). Where the analogy breaks: a virtual call on floor 2 already runs the top floor's method.' The aria-label lists the six steps in order. Keep all text at 11 px or larger so it reads at 390 px.
additions.why: The opening is about 400 words with no picture. This gives the page a single image (the construction floors) that the later sections, the VisualRecap and the flashcards ('Picture the floors') can all reuse. It turns the analogy text into a picture of the actual §8.7 order, with the analogy's breaking point marked on it.

additions.where: 'The rules you will rely on' (lines 75-80)
additions.what: Re-flow the four bullets into a 'Constructor rules at a glance' table with the columns 'You write | Allowed? | What happens, and why'. Keep every sentence and the Copying and Cloning link. Rows: (1) a class with no new: yes; the implicit constructor initializes the properties and does nothing else; in a subclass it first calls super.new() with no arguments unless extends Base(args) supplies them (§8.7, §8.17). (2) #, @ or wait inside new: no; new is a function and 'shall be nonblocking' (§8.7, §13.4 a); put the waiting in a task that runs after construction. (3) local or protected function new: yes; it limits who can call it (§8.18). (4) static or virtual function new: no (§8.7). (5) p2 = new p1;: yes, but it allocates the copy 'without calling the object's constructor or executing any variable declaration initialization' (§8.12 step 1). Optional verified row: (6) calling a task from new: no, because a function 'shall not enable tasks' (§13.4 b).
additions.why: It turns a list of rules into a grid the learner can scan, and it breaks the 350-word core stretch on lines 75-93. The legal and illegal cases now sit next to each other.

Each cell holds its real content from the Make It Work code: 1 base_item initializers: id and name get their defaults; 2 base_item body: count++, id = count, this.name = name, $display; 3 bus_item initializer: addr = 32'h100; 4 bus_item rest of body: $display addr; 5 crc_item initializer: crc = 8'h5a; 6 crc_item rest of body: $display crc. Below it, add a three-row <details> step reveal titled 'Map the three steps onto bus_item': step 1 = floors 1-2 (all of base_item, including its own base chain); step 2 = cell 3; step 3 = cell 4. A callout on the descending arrow reads 'super.new(...) arguments are evaluated here, before this floor's initializers (§8.7)', which sets up line 90 and the C/D prompt. Keep the existing C/D trace <details> and the crc_item SequenceDiagram unchanged.
additions.why: The core mental model (the §8.7 order) currently has a numbered list and a hidden table. This picture makes the order spatial, and it shows the abstract three-step rule on the concrete chain the page uses everywhere else.

additions.where: After the 'Read the diagram this way' paragraph (line 165), before '### `this`' (line 167)
additions.what: A predict-then-check about the third bug, using new names so that Kata 1 Break it 2 and quiz Q8 remain fresh checks. Add a 14-line `// snippet`: class base_chk whose new() calls init(); and declares 'virtual function void init(); endfunction'; class lim_chk extends base_chk, declares 'int limit = 5;', has no constructor, and overrides init() with $display("limit=%0d", limit). Caption: 'Dispatch goes to the object's class, but initialization follows §8.7 (§8.17 NOTE 2). Fix: call k.init() after new returns; it then prints limit=5.' The interview question at line 531 becomes the matching check later on the page.
additions.why: Objective 4's pitfall has no picture anywhere in Build Your Mental Model; it appears only in prose, the debugging table and the Recap. The diagram shows the exact moment dispatch reaches a floor that has no fixtures yet.

additions.where: 'this' section, between the bug/fix snippet (ends line 182) and 'Traced for p = new(5);' (line 184)
additions.what: A small scope picture as an inline SVG in <figure>/<figcaption> (role="img", with an aria-label that states the binding). The outer box is 'class Packet: property addr (int, default 0)'. Inside it, a nested box is 'function new(int addr = 0): argument addr = 5'. Inside the inner box are the two code lines 'addr = addr;' and 'this.addr = addr;'. Both names in 'addr = addr;' have arrows to the argument, labelled 'innermost scope wins (§8.11)'. The 'this.addr' name has an arrow out to the property, and the right-hand 'addr' has an arrow to the argument. Caption: 'An unqualified name resolves to the innermost scope, here the argument (§8.11), so addr = addr; never reaches the property.' Adjust the sentence at line 199 so it stays true without losing its fact, for example: 'The scope picture and the trace above are its picture, and the this.name = name step in base_item's body in the sequence diagram is the same pattern (there name is the argument "pkt0").'
additions.why: The trace table shows what the values become, and this picture shows why: the §8.11 innermost-scope rule. That rule is the second of the three Quick Take bugs, and quiz Q7 tests it.

additions.what: Add an 8-line `// snippet`: Base has 'int id; function new(int id = 0); this.id = id; endfunction'. Child extends Base and has 'function new(int id); $display("Child::new got id=%0d", id); endfunction', with no super.new. Caption: 'The base constructor is never skipped. With a required base argument the inserted call would not compile (row 1 of the table below).'
additions.why: This is the page's first and most common bug (silent defaults). The learner commits to an answer before the truth table, then sees the invisible inserted call drawn as a real arrow.

additions.where: 'Constant properties: set once', between 'Where an assignment to each kind of constant is legal:' (line 291) and the legality table (line 293)
additions.what: An <InterviewQuestionPlayground title="Predict: who may assign len?">. Question: 'jumbo_frame extends frame_item. Its constructor calls super.new(64); and then this.len = 9000;. What happens?'. Options, each with feedback: (correct) 'Compile error: len can be assigned only once, in the constructor of frame_item, the class that declares it (§8.19)'; 'len becomes 9000' (an instance constant gets one assignment, in its own class's constructor, §8.19); 'len stays 64 and the second assignment is ignored' (the compiler rejects it rather than dropping it); 'A run-time error when the constructor runs' (the violation is visible in the source, so it is a compile-time error). The table that follows is the check.
additions.why: The code comment already gives away the grow() case, so this asks about the subclass row, which learners usually get wrong. It makes the four-row table a check on a commitment rather than something to read passively.

additions.where: 'Debugging constructors: symptom, cause, fix', after the table (line 314)
additions.what: A 'match the symptom' <InterviewQuestionPlayground title="Debug it: a null error inside new">. Question: 'p = new; stops with a null-object error that points at hdr.len = 4; inside packet::new. packet declares header hdr; with no initializer. What is the cause?'. Options: 'p is still null while new runs' (wrong: the object under construction exists and this refers to it; the null handle is hdr, §8.4); (correct) 'hdr was never given an object, so hdr.len goes through null' (§8.4; fix with header hdr = new; as an initializer, or hdr = new; before first use, as the table's row says); 'A missing super.new' (wrong: the compiler always inserts it, §8.15, and it never causes a null access); 'A constructor may not touch handle properties' (wrong: it may, once they hold an object).
additions.why: It turns the seven-row symptom table into one diagnostic act, which practises the 'match the symptom, not the text' advice. It avoids the Break it 1 symptom, so Kata 1 stays fresh.

additions.where: Push Further, '### Expert: why UVM constructors have fixed signatures', after the three bullets (line 504)
additions.what: A table with the columns 'plain SV class | uvm_object subclass | uvm_component subclass'. Rows: your constructor (any argument list, §8.7 | function new(string name = "my_item"); super.new(name); | function new(string name, uvm_component parent); super.new(name, parent);); base constructor (your base's | uvm_object::new(string name=""), uvm_object.svh line 70 | uvm_component::new(string name, uvm_component parent), no defaults, uvm_component.svh line 76); who calls new (your code | the registry's create_object: new() if the name is empty, else new(name), uvm_registry.svh lines 194-202, and the create() that `uvm_object_utils defines, uvm_object_defines.svh lines 525-531 | the registry's create_component: new(name, parent), uvm_registry.svh line 73); extra arguments (allowed | only with defaults | only with defaults); no constructor written (implicit new calls super.new(), §8.7 | not covered on this page, so leave it as a dash and do not invent a claim | does not compile, as the bullet says); where children are built (your choice | not applicable | build_phase, not new, I-UVM-1C).

additions.where: Same subsection, right after the comparison table
additions.what: Two compact SequenceDiagrams with four participants each. (a) title="How the factory calls an object's constructor": factory -> uvm_object_registry #(my_item) 'create_object(name)'; registry -> my_item::new 'new() if name == "", else new(name)'; my_item::new -> uvm_object::new 'super.new(name)'; returns. Caption: uvm_registry.svh lines 194-202; the factory calls create_object after it has chosen the type (the comment at lines 186-191). (b) title="How the factory calls a component's constructor": factory -> uvm_component_registry #(my_drv) 'create_component(name, parent)'; registry -> my_drv::new 'new(name, parent)' (uvm_registry.svh line 73); my_drv::new -> uvm_component::new 'super.new(name, parent)'; returns; then a note with tone error spanning my_drv::new to uvm_component::new: 'no new in my_drv: the implicit new() calls super.new() with no arguments, but uvm_component::new has no defaults, so it does not compile (§8.7)'.
additions.why: The section describes generated call chains in prose only. Drawing them shows exactly which argument list your constructor must accept and where the implicit-constructor failure happens.

newComponentRequests: ConstructorChainVisualizer (planned in lesson-plans-2026-10-28 but absent from the component backlog; not built). It needs a pure model, src/lib/sv-constructor-model.ts, reusing ancestry/resolveCall from sv-object-model.ts. The model covers classes with extends; properties with initializer expressions that may read other properties; constructor arguments with defaults; super.new argument expressions; an optional extends Base(args) clause; a missing super.new (draw the compiler-inserted super.new() as a greyed line); and an optional virtual call inside a constructor. State per property is a value or 'undefined', drawn hatched with a dash, and undefined spreads through any expression that reads it. An optional overlay labelled 'tool-dependent: most simulators print 0' is never presented as the rule. A compile-check pass with clauses rejects: a required argument missing from the inserted or implicit super.new (§8.7, §8.15); super.new that is not the first executable statement (§8.17); extends arguments combined with an explicit super.new (§8.17); an instance const assigned outside its class's constructor (§8.19); and a static or virtual constructor (§8.7). The view draws stacked class layers with the root at the bottom, matching the lesson's floors picture, plus a call-stack strip, CodeTrace, What/Why narration, a log panel and a static count box, with PredictionPrompt gates at the decisive steps. Presets: lrm-cd (§8.7: c1=1, c2=2, c3 undefined, d1=4, d2=2, d3=6, checked against the LRM text), three-level (base_item/bus_item/crc_item with the log), missing-super (Child new(7) gives c.id = 0), required-arg (compile error), extends-clause, virtual-in-ctor (base_item::new calls describe()), kata2 and kata2-stretch (super.new(w) spreads undefined). Modes: trace, experiment (toggles inside the code lines) and debug (Kata 1 logs, pick the suspect and the fix, HintLadder). Props: preset?, presets?, mode?. Embed points on this page: construction order (lrm-cd, three-level), super chaining (missing-super, experiment), the virtual-call pitfall (virtual-in-ctor), Make It Work (three-level with log), Kata 1 (debug) and Kata 2 (fill in the table).

The new preset's packet constructor runs count++; id = count; with a const id, so stepping through p1 = new; p2 = new; p3 = new p1; shows count staying at 2 while p3.id equals p1.id (§8.9, §8.12 step 1, §8.19). textHeavy: Lines 15-26, Quick Take plus 'You will be able to' (about 420 words of prose, nothing visual before <BeforeYouStart /> at line 28). Covers class, object and handle (§8.4), why most testbench class bugs are handle bugs, and the house-address analogy with its three breaking points: a blank card is null, there is no arithmetic on a handle (Table 8-1), and there is no delete (§8.29).

Lines 195-211, the longest stretch in Build Your Mental Model (about 450 words). additions.where: ### Your first class, right after the 'One trap from Tier 1' paragraph (line 105)
additions.what: Priority medium. A one-line 'Predict first' prompt with two questions, then one <details className="my-4 rounded-xl border border-border/70 p-3"><summary className="cursor-pointer font-semibold">Check your predictions</summary> holding both answers. (1) 'In the packet constructor, change this.addr = addr; to addr = addr;. What does pkt1.print() show?' Answer: packet addr=0x00000000 data=0x0000cafe. The unqualified addr resolves to the innermost scope, the argument (§8.11, verified: 'an unqualified reference to x shall be resolved by looking at the innermost scope, in this case, the subroutine argument declaration'). The statement copies the argument onto itself, so the property keeps its default 0. It compiles, with no error. (2) 'Inside an initial block, does packet p = new; compile? What changes with static or automatic in front?' Answer: without a keyword it is illegal (§6.21: 'an explicit static keyword shall be required when an initialization value is specified'). static packet p = new; builds one object, once, at the beginning of simulation, even inside a loop. automatic packet p = new; runs every time the declaration is reached (the §6.21 example shows automatic int loop3 = 0; with the comment 'executes every loop'). Link to Constructors for the scope picture of this.addr vs addr, rather than drawing it here.
additions.why: Turns the two densest rules in the 260-word bullet run (98-105) into checks the learner commits to. The addr = addr bug is one of the three constructor bugs the module tests, and the §6.21 trap catches Tier 1 habits.

additions.where: ### Class anatomy, after the 'const properties' bullet (line 148), before '### Static members' (line 150)
additions.what: Priority medium. An <InterviewQuestionPlayground title="Check: which out-of-block body compiles?">. Question: 'Inside bus_txn you add extern virtual function kind_e peek(bit verbose = 0);. Which body, written after the class, compiles?' Options and feedback: (a) function kind_e bus_txn::peek(bit verbose = 0); is wrong: kind_e is declared inside the class, so the return type must be written bus_txn::kind_e (§8.24: 'the class scope resolution operator shall be used to indicate the internal return type'). (b) function bus_txn::kind_e bus_txn::peek(bit verbose); is correct: the return type is scoped, virtual is dropped, and a default value in the prototype may be omitted in the body (§8.24). (c) function bus_txn::kind_e bus_txn::peek(bit verbose = 1); is wrong: a default written in the body must be syntactically identical to the prototype's (§8.24). (d) virtual function bus_txn::kind_e bus_txn::peek(bit verbose = 0); is wrong: qualifiers such as virtual, local and protected go only on the prototype. The out-of-block function_declaration grammar (A.2.6: function [dynamic_override_specifiers] [lifetime] function_body_declaration) has no place for them (§8.24). All four rules were checked in t1_lrm_clean.txt §8.24 and the A.2.6 production.
additions.why: The four 'extern rules the compiler enforces' (line 147) are pure rule text. A per-option-feedback check makes the learner apply each rule to a concrete line, which is what they need when a compiler rejects an out-of-block body.

additions.where: Where null handles come from, after 'The guard' snippet (line 242), before '### Encapsulation' (244)
additions.what: Priority medium (keep it compact). A one-glance table, 'Four null sources at a glance'. Columns: Cause | What the log shows (wording is tool-dependent) | Guard. Rows: (1) Missing new | a null-object error at the first member access through that handle; for a non-virtual method call, usually inside the method | construct before use; if (h == null) $fatal at the boundary. (2) Built inside a subroutine | the caller's handle is still null after the call; the error appears at the caller's first access | return the handle, or use an output or ref argument (§13.5.2). (3) Unset vif | a fatal null virtual-interface error at the first vif access, which the standard requires (§25.9) | set it before first use; guard in the driver. (4) Unchecked $cast, function form | no error at the cast; the destination is left unchanged (often null), and the error appears later, at its first use (§6.24.2). The task form gives a run-time error at the cast itself | if (!$cast(dst, src)) $fatal(...). Link row 4 to Polymorphism Pitfalls' '$cast as a function or as a task' section; verify the heading slug with check-mdx. Every fact is already in items 1-4 or the Make It Work table.

Virtual method | illegal (§8.4) | fails at the call, because finding the body needs the object. Null virtual interface | 'shall result in a fatal run-time error' (§25.9) | a fatal error at the first access. §8.4, §8.9 and §25.9 wording verified in t1_lrm_clean.txt.

Edges: strong->weak, style 'causal', label 'GC'; weak->gone, style 'causal', label 'cleared'; strong->gone, style 'causal', label 'no refs', via [[1,1.5]] or similar (check for label-on-node); roots->strong, style 'structural', label 'keeps'. Caption: 'Garbage collection moves an object from strongly reachable to unreachable, through weakly reachable if a weak_reference refers to it. When a referent is weakly reachable, all weak references to it are cleared atomically (§8.30.1). Only then is the memory eligible for reclamation; when it is actually freed is up to the implementation.' Verified against §8.29 (the three definitions; 'eligible for reclamation once the object becomes unreachable') and §8.30.1 ('shall clear all weak references to that referent... performed atomically').

textHeavy: L17-28, Quick Take and 'You will be able to' (about 390 words of prose, nothing visual before <BeforeYouStart/> at L29). Covers the three kinds of 'copy' (p2 = p1 copies the handle; p2 = new p1 is a shallow copy, §8.12; a deep copy is a user-written copy()/clone()), why it matters (a scoreboard's stored data changes with no error), the folder / sticky-note / drawer analogy and where it breaks (a non-virtual clone() builds the wrong class), and four objectives. The first table is at L39 and the first picture at L54.

L88-99 (about 265 words, just under the threshold but dense). Covers §8.12's shallow copy as five numbered rules: the source object's class is allocated; no constructor or declaration initializer runs; properties are copied as values, including randomization state; class handles are copied as handles; a queue of handles gets its own container holding the same handles. Then two syntax rules (Syntax 8-2; no typed constructor call, §8.8). No code or picture appears until L100, and the rules are pictured only by the trace table at L136.

L262-276 (about 340 words). Covers '### Comparing copies: == asks the same object?' (== and != compare handles, §11.4.5; a scoreboard 'exp == act' gives false mismatches and false matches; compare() by value; the debugging hint) and the start of '### clone()' (why clone() exists, and its three requirements: clone() virtual and overridden, copy() virtual, the subclass copy() keeps the base argument type and uses $cast, §8.20). The == subsection has no code, no table and no picture.

L376-391 (about 315 words). Covers four 'What goes wrong without each piece' bullets (clone() not virtual, no override in the subclass, no super.copy(rhs), an unchecked $cast, and the task form being a run-time error, §6.24.2), then the four bullets of 'How UVM splits the same job' (clone() = create(get_name()) + copy(this); create() from the utils macro; copy() non-virtual with OBJ/COPY and the copier; do_copy() the hook, IEEE 1800.2-2020 §5.3.8.2). These failure modes are only described; none is shown.

L642-699 (about 1,200 words, the longest stretch on the page, with no code, table or picture). Covers the Break 2 explanation (compare from the side whose class has the most fields), the seven-step 'How to add copy support to a class', the checklist, and all five Push Further expert subsections: what else a shallow copy copies (RNG state, rand_mode, constraint_mode, randc state, the embedded covergroup set to null, instance constants, the class follows the object; §8.12, §18.14.3, §19.4, §8.19); override rules (§8.20 matching arguments, covariant return, §8.18 local per class, :extends/:final); back-pointers and shared sub-objects, and uvm_copier's recursion tracking; ownership, copying at one end and cost; and why UVM separates copy() from do_copy().

Minor: L450-466 (about 200 words). The five Recap bullets and the Make It Work intro, with no recap picture; the lesson has no VisualRecap. L975-1000 is References, citations rather than teaching prose, so it is not flagged.

additions.where: ## Push Further, ### Expert: what else a shallow copy copies (L665-671), after the intro line
additions.what: A table with the columns Aspect | p2 = new p1 (shallow) | p2 = p1.clone() (new + copy()). Rows: constructor and declaration initializers: not run (§8.12 step 1) | run by new (§8.7). Class of the new object: the source object's class (§8.12) | the class clone() constructs (the object's class when clone() is virtual and overridden). RNG state: copied, so the next randomize() calls should pick the same values (§8.12, §18.14.3) | a fresh RNG seeded from the creating thread (§18.14.3); copy() does not move RNG state. rand_mode, constraint_mode, randc cyclic state: copied (§8.12 step 2) | the new object's own; random variables and constraints start active (§18.8, §18.9) unless copy() sets them. Embedded covergroup: set to null, and the copy's properties are not covered (§8.12 step 2 and NOTE) | exists only if the constructor builds it; it may be assigned only in new() (§19.4), so copy() cannot set it. Instance constant (const int uid): copied (§8.12, §8.19) | assigned once by the constructor; copy() cannot assign it (§8.19). Nested objects: shared (§8.12) | as deep as copy() is written.
additions.why: This expert subsection is four dense bullets in the 1,200-word wall, and every bullet is a 'shallow vs clone' contrast, so the table matches its shape. Re-verified in t1_lrm_clean.txt: §8.12 step 2 lists the RNG state, constraint_mode, rand_mode and randc state, and the embedded covergroup set to null; §18.14.3 says the seed 'is taken from the parent thread when the instance is created'; §18.8 and §18.9 say 'initially active'; §19.4 says 'The covergroup variable shall not be assigned outside the new() method'; §8.19 says instance constants are assigned only once, in the constructor.

additions.where: ### Expert: override rules that shape copy() and clone() (L673-678)
additions.what: A table with the columns Rule | Legal | Illegal | Clause. Rows: argument types, names, qualifiers and directions must match: crc_packet: virtual function void copy(packet rhs); | copy(crc_packet rhs), or copy(packet src) with a renamed argument | §8.20. The return type may be a derived class: virtual function crc_packet clone(); | a return type that is neither matching nor derived (for example header) | §8.20. local is per class, not per object: inside crc_packet::copy, r.secret where secret is local to crc_packet | from crc_packet, reading rhs.secret where secret is local to packet ('local members are not visible within subclasses') | §8.18. Override specifiers: virtual function :extends void copy(packet rhs); | :extends on a method that overrides no virtual base method, e.g. a misspelled cpy (an error); overriding a :final method | §8.20, with support tool-dependent per the lesson.
additions.why: Four rule bullets with code fragments are easier to apply as legal/illegal pairs. Each row is verified in §8.20 ('matching argument types, identical argument names, identical qualifiers, and identical directions'; return type 'a matching type ... or a derived class type'; Example 3 for :extends/:final) and §8.18.

additions.where: ### Expert: deep copies of linked and shared structures (L680-684), after the 'Shared sub-objects' bullet
additions.what: A <details> check: 'b1.beats holds header h1 and h2, and b1.last_beat = h2. Predict, for a naive deep copy() and for a correct one: how many header objects does the copy own, and what is copy.last_beat == copy.beats[1]?' Reveal a 2-row table: naive (deep-copies beats and then last_beat separately): 3 headers, == gives 0, so the copy's shape differs from the original's. Correct (copy once, then point last_beat at the copy of beats[1]): 2 headers, == gives 1. Optionally add a small inline SVG with the three panels original / naive / correct.
additions.why: The shape-changing bug is easy to state and hard to picture. A predict step that ends in counting boxes makes it concrete, and it uses == on handles, the identity test from earlier in the page, in a case where identity is exactly what you want. The facts restate the lesson's bullet.

additions.where: ### Expert: deep copies of linked and shared structures, after the 'Back-pointers' bullet (L682)
additions.what: A SequenceDiagram titled 'A naive deep copy of a back-pointer never returns'. Participants: tb_top, 'burst copy' (b2), 'beat copy' (b2.beats[0]), 'new parent' (a burst built inside beat::copy). Messages: b2.copy(b1); a self-message 'beats[0] = new; copy(rhs.beats[0])'; beat::copy runs 'parent = new; parent.copy(rhs.parent)' with tone 'error'; the new parent copies its beats again; a divider '... repeats: each level builds a new burst and new beats'. Then an error-tone note: 'never returns; how the run ends is tool-dependent'. A last note gives the fix: 'copy parent as a handle, or set it to the new burst after copying the children'. Optionally mention in the caption that uvm_copier records started/finished pairs (m_recur_states in uvm_copier.svh copy_object).
additions.why: Unbounded recursion is a call-flow problem, and a sequence diagram is the house picture for call chains. It turns 'the copy recurses' into something the learner can see grow. Every runtime outcome is labelled tool-dependent, and the uvm_copier detail is verified (uvm_copier.svh L86-112).

additions.where: ### Expert: ownership, cost and where copies belong (L686-690), after the 'One rule for every channel' bullet

additions.where: ### Kata: four bugs in one clone, inside the worked-solution <details> (L913-974), one diagram after each task's log
additions.what: Four small heap ArchitectureDiagrams (2x2 grid: orig and q in column 0, header@1 and header@2 in column 1, hdr edges, legend={false}), one per task, so the learner can check their drawing after each fix. Bins: assign the value / deep-copy the owned object (mirror null, call copy()) / rebuild the queue element by element / copy the handle on purpose with a comment (shared resource or back-pointer) / cannot be set by copy() (instance constant, §8.19; embedded covergroup, assignable only in new(), §19.4). additions.where: ### Why generic classes, after the paragraph 'A parameterized class removes both problems...' (L41)
additions.what: P1. Table 'Three ways to hold three item types' with columns: Copy the class per type | Store a base-class handle (base q[$]) | Parameterized class fifo #(T). findings: S2 line 829 - The singleton SequenceDiagram caption says 'Only code inside tb_registry can call its protected new (§8.18), so get() is the only way in'. That describes local, not protected. §8.18 says a protected member 'can be inherited; it is visible to subclasses', and the lesson says the same at line 807 ('A protected constructor allows subclasses but blocks new from outside the class'). A subclass's super.new() can call it, so the caption contradicts both the clause it cites and the lesson text about the local vs protected difference. -> Reword to: 'Only tb_registry and its subclasses can call its protected new (§8.18); outside code cannot, so it must go through get(), and every such caller shares one object.'

S3 line 801 - In the virtual-call comparison table, the Java cell 'As in SystemVerilog' on the row 'Can it rely on the derived class's initialized fields?' brings in the SV reason ('undefined until their initializers run'). Java default-initializes fields (0/null) before any constructor runs, so they are not undefined. This is also a new claim beyond the lesson's 'Java behaves like SystemVerilog', which is about dispatch only. -> Change the Java cell to 'No: its initializers have not run yet', or limit the Java column to the dispatch row.

S3 line 604 - The UVM table row 'Base constructor it chains to' lists uvm_object::new / uvm_component::new for '(transaction, configuration)' and '(driver, monitor)'. additions.where: ### External constraint blocks, after the 'Why use them?' paragraph (line 111), before 'Two details matter'.
additions.what: A 'Will it compile?' prompt with six short snippets in a list, then <details className="my-4 rounded-xl border border-border/70 p-3"><summary>Check your verdicts</summary> with a verdict table (Snippet | Verdict | Clause). (a) class A with extern constraint c; and no A::c anywhere: error (§18.5.1). (b) class B with constraint c; and no body: compiles; c is an empty constraint (as the constant 1); a warning may be issued (§18.5.1). (c) constraint C::c { x > 0; } written above class C in the same module: error, the body must come after the class (§18.5.1). (d) class D with both constraint c; and constraint c { x > 0; } inside it: error (§18.5.1). (e) two bodies constraint E::c { ... } for one prototype: error (§18.5.1). (f) extern static constraint c; in class F but body constraint F::c { ... } without static: error, static on both or neither (§18.5.10). Note the syntax order for (f): the qualifier comes first, 'extern static constraint c;' (Syntax A.1.10 constraint_prototype).
additions.why: Objective 1 asks the learner to predict what happens when a body is missing, duplicated or misplaced, but the page only states the rules. Applying the table to code is the active step; the verdicts are all verified against §18.5.1 and §18.5.10.

additions.where: ### External constraint blocks, after 'Two details matter for soft constraints and static blocks' (line 113).
additions.what: A worked micro-example of the prototype-position rule. Snippet: class g_item; rand bit [3:0] x; constraint c_a { soft x == 1; } extern constraint c_b; constraint c_c { soft x == 3; } endclass, then constraint g_item::c_b { soft x == 2; } written after the class. Prompt: 'The body of c_b is written last. What is x?' Reveal in <details>: 'x is 3 on every call. c_b ranks at its prototype, second in the class, so c_c (third) outranks it and c_a ranks lowest; all three conflict, so only c_c is kept (§18.5.13.1). Move the prototype below c_c and x becomes 2.' Add a pointer: 'This is the external-block rung of the priority ladder below.'
additions.why: The rule 'ranked by the prototype, not the body' is the least intuitive line of the priority table, and the page states it twice without an example. It mirrors the standard's own d1 < e1 < f1 ordering.

additions.where: ### Bound every array size, after the three rules (line 133), before 'A queue declared rand is resized at the back'.
additions.what: <SequenceDiagram title="One randomize() of packet: size first, then elements">. Participants: 'test code' (generic), 'solver' (generic), 'p.data[]' (generic). Messages: call test code -> solver 'p.randomize()'; self solver 'pick len and data.size() (c_len, c_size)'; call solver -> p.data[] 'resize to len (§18.4)'; call solver -> p.data[] 'randomize every element'; note solver..p.data[] 'foreach rules on elements are solved after the size (§18.5.7.1)'; return solver -> test code '1'; divider 'Same call, no size constraint'; self solver 'size not constrained: no resize'; call solver -> p.data[] 'randomize existing elements only'; note solver..p.data[] 'a new object's empty array stays empty (§18.4)'. Caption: 'The size is fixed before any element is chosen, so the number of possible payloads never weights len. With no size constraint, or only a discarded soft one, the array keeps its size (§18.4).'
additions.why: Both array rules (sizes first, and no constraint means no resize, quiz Q3 and Q4) are prose only, inside a 285-word run. A two-phase call picture is exactly what a learner needs to recall when a payload comes out empty.

additions.where: ### Bound every array size, after 'A queue declared rand is resized at the back ... never randomized (§18.4)' (line 135).
additions.what: Table 'What randomize() does to each kind of rand array'. Columns: Array kind | Size randomized? | How the size changes | Elements. Rows: dynamic array T d[] | yes, if size() is constrained | resized; the resized array is initialized with the original contents (§18.4, §7.5.1) | all randomized. Queue T q[$] | yes, if size() is constrained | elements inserted or deleted at the back (right side); new elements start at the type's default (§18.4) | all randomized. Associative array | never; size and indices are not randomizable (§18.4) | unchanged | existing elements randomized. Fixed-size unpacked array | no, fixed by the declaration | unchanged | all randomized (§18.4). A one-line note under it: an array of class handles is resized but randomize() never allocates objects; new slots are null (§18.4).
additions.why: The two sentences at line 135 compress four different behaviours; a table makes them comparable at a glance. Every cell is taken from §18.4 (checked in t1_lrm_clean.txt).

additions.what: Under the six-step list, add a mapping table: Step | Where the bench does it | Clause. 1 | c_len and c_size, one rule per named block | §18.5. 2 | extern constraint c_addr; and constraint base_item::c_addr after the class | §18.5.1. 3 | c_size ties data.size() to len, and c_len bounds len to 1..16 | §18.4. 4 | c_def in base_item, c_long in long_item, the two inline with calls; the kata's guarded !is_err -> soft len == 16 | §18.5.13.1. 5 | err_item vs err_item_ordered after counting 257 pairs | §18.5.9. 6 | if (!x.randomize()) $fatal(...) and the n_def, n_long, n_err counters | §18.6.1.

additions.where: ## Push Further, ### Expert: disable soft and the soft dist trap (lines 364-370), after the three bullets.
additions.what: A 'Predict x' table with the result column hidden in <details>. Visible column: constraints in declaration order. Rows: (1) soft x == 3; disable soft x; soft x inside {1, 2}; (2) soft x == 3; disable soft x; (3) soft x == 5; then in a later block soft x dist {5, 8}; (4) soft x == 5; then disable soft x; soft x dist {5, 8}; (5) with rand p, q: p -> soft q; soft !p || q; disable soft p. Revealed: (1) 1 or 2 (§18.5.13.2, the standard's A1/A2/A3); (2) unconstrained; (3) always 5, nothing conflicts so both are kept (§18.5.13.1 property 2); (4) 5 or 8, equally likely (the standard's B example); (5) soft !p || q is discarded, p -> soft q is kept, because disable soft acts only where the variable appears directly.
additions.why: The soft dist trap is a classic interview item and is currently a bullet. Predicting all five rows side by side shows the one rule (disable soft discards lower soft constraints regardless of conflict) by contrast.

additions.where: ## Push Further, ### Expert: soft priorities across contained objects and loops, after 'The standard's worked example ... ranks fourteen soft constraints' (line 380).
additions.what: Add the standard's B1/D1/B2/D2 example as a // snippet (a: soft x > 10, soft x < 100; b: soft x inside {[5:9]}; c: soft y > 10; d: soft y inside {[5:9]}; prototype constraint e; declared after d, body D2::e { soft y > 100; }; rand D1 p1; rand B1 p2; rand D1 p3; f: soft p1.x < p2.x; inline with { soft y inside {10,20,30}; soft y < p1.x; }). Prompt: 'Where does e1 rank against d1? Where does c1 rank against p3.b1?' Then <details> with a banded table, highest first: 1-2 i2, i1 (inline; later above earlier) | 3 f1 (D2 block declared after prototype e) | 4 e1 (external body, ranked at its prototype, after d) | 5 d1 | 6 c1 (base class B2, below derived D2) | 7-9 p3.b1, p3.a2, p3.a1 (contained; handle p3 declared last; derived b above base a; a2 later than a1) | 10-11 p2.a2, p2.a1 | 12-14 p1.b1, p1.a2, p1.a1. Last line: if p1 and p3 refer to the same object, the p1 rows disappear and 11 remain, because the object takes the priority of the handle declared last.
additions.why: The page refers to the standard's 14-rung example without showing it. The banded table is the static fallback for the missing ladder interactive, and each band names the rule that puts it there (checked against §18.5.13.1 in t1_lrm_clean.txt).

additions.where: ## Push Further, ### Expert: external blocks with static and override specifiers (lines 382-386), after the bullets.
additions.what: Table with columns Qualifier | With a prototype and an external body | Other rules | Clause. static | on both or on neither | constraint_mode() then affects every instance; may not be combined with :initial, :extends or :final (Syntax 18-9, footnote 11) | §18.5.10. :initial / :extends / :final | on both or on neither | :initial must not override, :extends must override, the two are mutually exclusive; :final forbids further replacement and may combine with either | §18.5.2. pure constraint c; | prototype-like, only in a virtual (abstract) class | every non-abstract derived class must provide c (block, or prototype plus external body); :final is illegal on a pure constraint (Syntax A.1.10, footnote 8); a pure constraint may be static, and the overriding constraint must match | §18.5.2, §18.5.10. Keep 'Tool support for these newer specifiers varies (tool-dependent)' under the table.
additions.why: Three bullets pack about a dozen both-or-neither and may-combine rules; a table makes them scannable for interview review. All rows verified in §18.5.2, §18.5.10 and Annex A footnotes 8 and 11.

additions.where: ## Push Further, ### Expert: how solve...before is actually applied (lines 388-393), after the last bullet.
additions.what: Table 'Orderings that can and cannot make randomize() fail'. Columns: Ordering | Who imposes it | What it does | Can make randomize() fail? | Clause. solve a before b | you | reshapes the odds over the same legal set | no | §18.5.9. randc variables first | implicit | the randc set is solved before the rest | yes, sometimes | §18.4.2. Array sizes before foreach | implicit | size() is a state variable inside the foreach | yes, in some situations | §18.5.7.1. Random function arguments before the call | implicit | subdivides the solution space; later constraints see fixed values | yes | §18.5.11. Link I-SV-2B solver debug under it.
additions.why: It contrasts the one ordering the learner writes with the three the language imposes, which is the bridge to I-SV-2B solver debug. Each 'can fail' cell is a direct statement in the cited clause.

additions.where: ## Push Further, ### Expert: interview angles, the 'soft len < 6' prompt (line 409).
additions.what: Add a second <InterviewQuestionPlayground title="Interview: three soft defaults"> with the prompt's question and options: '4 on every call' (correct: the inline soft constraint is top and conflicts with c_long, so c_long is dropped; len == 4 fits len < 6, so c_def is kept; a soft constraint is dropped only when it conflicts, §18.5.13.1); 'uniform over 1..5' (only if c_def were dropped, but nothing above it conflicts with it); 'uniform over 8..16' (c_long ranks below the inline constraint and conflicts with it); 'randomize() fails' (conflicts between soft constraints never make a call fail). Keep the existing bullet but move its parenthetical answer into a <details> reveal so it no longer sits under the question.
additions.why: The prompt is the best test of the ladder (a lower rung survives because it does not conflict), but its answer is printed next to it. An MCQ with diagnostic feedback turns it into practice.

No default at all, no c_order | 65 (64 with is_err = 0, plus (1, 1)) | 1/65 ≈ 1.5% | 1/65. No default, with c_order | the same 65 | 1/2 | 1/128.

The first picture of any kind is the code block at line 40.

Lines 70-93 (about 485 words): reads the packet class line by line (rand is uniform when unconstrained §18.4.1, constraint blocks §18.5, inside with $ bounds and the empty reversed range §11.4.13, the randomize() return value §18.6.1), then the three §18.3 rules, state variables (§18.5.8 step c), 'the two mistakes everyone makes first' and the solution-space intro, all before the stepper at line 95.

Lines 97-106 (about 293 words): the stepper debrief, then a four-item to-do list for the heatmap's coupling, dist, soft and debug scenarios. It sets up dist, soft and failure work long before the sections that teach them.

Misconception 4 has no picture beyond the table.

Lines 252-284 (about 640 words, the longest stretch on the core path): the implication/external-block pointer, all of 'Reading dist weights' (:= vs :/ on ranges, ratios, dist as a membership constraint, coupled dist), all of 'solve…before changes the odds' (§18.5.9 semantics and restrictions) and the opening of 'soft' (hard vs soft, the three §18.5.13.1 priority rules). These are three separate mental models, and spine misconceptions 1-3, with no visual until the Config code at line 288.

Lines 378-384 (about 195 words, borderline): the two unsafe call forms (void'/bare call §13.4.1; assert with assertions off §20.11 or on §16.3) and the three implicit solve orders that can fail (§18.4.2, §18.5.7.1, §18.5.11). There is no side-by-side picture of what each call form does on a failure.

Lines 494-512 (about 300 words): 'Why each line looks the way it does' (six output-to-rule bullets), 'Run it' and the six-step adaptation list. The link between each output line and its constraint is prose only.

Lines 539-565 (about 570 words): the 'In a UVM testbench' paragraph after its code, the six-item checklist, the Push Further intro and the six dist corner-case bullets (additive weights, := counting excluded values in 1800-2023, default :/, weights from state variables, limits, coupled dist). additions.where: ## Quick Take, directly after 'The Analogy' bullet (line 19), before 'You will be able to'
additions.what: A 'stencil map' <figure> holding an inline SVG (viewBox about 360x260, style width 100%, maxWidth 360; role=img with a full aria-label; page-unique ids prefixed isv2a-) and a <figcaption>. It has four panels on one shared 4x4 grid motif. (1) 'Hard constraints = the stencil': open cells marked ✓ and closed cells marked ✕, with one dart in an open cell, captioned 'each call lands in one open hole, all equally likely (§18.5.9)'. (2) 'dist and solve…before = the odds': the same open cells drawn as larger or smaller dots or hatched, with one row closed and labelled 'dist: unlisted values closed'. (3) 'soft = tape': a tape strip over the cells the default excludes, labelled 'kept on every call; peeled off whole only if no hole would stay open'. (4) 'randc = a deck per object': cards 2, 0, 3 dealt and one card left face down. A footer reads 'no open hole: randomize() returns 0 and keeps the old values'. Each panel title names the section that teaches it, so the figure also serves as the page roadmap the 'How to read this lesson' paragraph describes. The caption labels it a conceptual illustration (◇) and repeats where it breaks: the solver never lists holes one by one, randc remembers earlier darts, and soft is all or nothing. Use currentColor and mid-tone theme-safe colours, with non-colour cues (✓/✕, hatch, the tape outline).
additions.why: This is the first picture on the page, after about 430 words of bullets. It turns the analogy into one image of the lesson's four tools and the failure case, and that same image comes back as the closing recap (see the Practice & Reinforce item), so learners recall the whole page by one picture.

additions.where: ### Your first random class, after the `randomize()` bullet (line 75), before 'Three rules from §18.3'
additions.what: A number-line strip <figure> (inline SVG) for `rand bit [7:0] len`, drawn as a 0..20 window with a break mark '…255'. Three rows, each filling the cells it allows (a filled square plus the value, not colour alone): `len inside {[1:16]}` gives 1..16; `len inside {0, [4:7], 12}` gives 0, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 12; `len inside {[$:3]}` gives 0..3, labelled '$ = the lowest value of bit [7:0], 0'. The caption says every member is equally likely inside a constraint (§18.5.3). Then a one-line prompt, 'Predict: what does randomize() return with len inside {[16:8]}?', followed by <details className="my-4 rounded-xl border border-border/70 p-3"> holding a fourth, empty row and the answer: 0 on every call, because a range whose left bound is greater than its right is empty (§11.4.13), so no len is legal (§18.6.1). Verified against IEEE 1800-2023 §11.4.13: '$ shall represent the lowest or highest value for the type of the expression on the left-hand side' and 'If the bound to the left of the colon is greater than the bound to the right, the range is empty'.
additions.why: It pictures set membership and both traps the bullet states in one dense sentence ($ bounds, the reversed range). The reversed-range quiz question (Q10) and the Mistakes-table row then have an image to recall.

additions.where: ### Your first random class, after the state-variable paragraph (line 83), before 'The two mistakes everyone makes first'
additions.what: A two-column table, 'Random variable' vs 'State variable'. Row 'Declared as': a `rand` or `randc` class property / anything else a constraint reads (a non-rand property, a caller's variable or argument, or a rand variable switched off with `rand_mode(0)`, which I-SV-2B teaches, §18.8). Row 'May the solver change it?': yes, a new value on each successful call / no, its current value is used as a constant (§18.5.8 step c). Row 'On this page': `opcode`, `len`, `tag` / the `rd_w`, `wr_w` weight knobs in the pattern table and the `send_len` argument read through `local::len`. Verified: §18.5.8 c) 'All other variable references are treated as state variables, whose current value is used as a constant'; §18.8 'their values are treated as state variables by the solver'.
additions.why: State variables come back four times later (dist weight knobs, local::len, the heatmap's rand_mode toggle, the solver-debug link), and right now they get a single sentence. The table gives the distinction a shape learners can find again.

additions.where: ### The solver picks one legal combination, the heatmap embed at line 108 and the to-do list at lines 99-106
additions.what: Narrow the embed to `<ConstraintSolverHeatmapVisualizer initialScenario="coupling" scenarios={["coupling"]} />`. Keep the lead sentence ('commit to a number for P(x == 0)'), item 1 (Coupled variables, c_order) and 'Then run 1,000 calls…' here. Move items 2 (dist), 3 (soft) and 4 (debug) word for word to the dist, soft and failure sections, each beside its own single-scenario embed (next items), and replace 'Work through the scenarios in order:' with a one-line pointer saying that the dist, soft and failure sections each open this heatmap on their own scenario. additions.where: ### randc: one permutation per object, after the 'What the table shows' bullets (line 171), before 'Pitfalls and limits'
additions.what: A 'one deck per object' <figure> (inline SVG, four small panels, role=img and a full aria-label). (1) Two decks, a and b. a has dealt 2, 0, 3 (face up, struck through) and holds 1 face down, labelled 'call 4: only 1'. b has its own order, 1, 3, 0, with 2 left. (2) A cycle boundary: a's run reads 2 0 3 1 | 1 …, with the second 1 marked 'repeat across a boundary: allowed'. (3) static randc: arrows from a and b into one shared deck, labelled 'one sequence for every instance'. (4) A new item per transaction: three fresh full decks, item1, item2 and item3, labelled 'a fresh deck each time, so tags can repeat'. Caption: '§18.4.2. The permutation is also recomputed when the constraints on the variable change (rows 6 and 7 of the table).' Draw it in the site's own layout; do not copy the standard's Figure 18-1 rows. Verified against §18.4.2 (permutation recomputed 'whenever the constraints change on that variable or when none of the remaining values … can satisfy the constraints'; 'If a random variable is declared as static, the randc state … shall also be static').
additions.why: This is spine misconception 4 (randc cycles across objects), and the 367 words after the trace table have no picture. A deck per object is a picture learners can carry to the UVM 'new item per transaction' trap, and to the interview question in Push Further.

additions.where: ### Constraint blocks, inside and common patterns, inside the is_read <details> reveal, after the paragraph that adds `solve is_read before len` (line 249)
additions.what: A 'same cells, different odds' proportional strip (inline SVG, about 340 wide), with two rows of the same 43 legal (is_read, len) pairs. Top row, no ordering: 43 equal segments, with the one is_read = 1 segment (len = 8) outlined and starred, labelled '1/43 ≈ 2.3%'. Bottom row, solve is_read before len: the same 43 segments, now with (1, 8) half the bar wide (1/2) and each of the 42 is_read = 0 segments 1/84 wide (≈ 1.2%). Caption: 'Both rows hold the same 43 legal pairs; ordering changes only their widths (probabilities), never which pairs exist (§18.5.9).' Numbers checked: c_len allows 9 + 33 = 42 lengths, and is_read = 1 forces len = 8, so 43 pairs; ordered, 1/2 and 1/2 × 1/42 = 1/84. This matches the standard's own s -> d == 0 example (Table 18-1 vs Table 18-2).
additions.why: It shows misconception 3 ('solve…before changes what is legal') on the lesson's own example: same cells, new widths. The same strip style is reused in the kata solution, so 'ordering reweights, never relegalises' is one recurring picture.

additions.where: ### Reading dist weights, after the paragraph 'So opcode is 0 on 10% of calls…' (line 264)
additions.what: A stacked weight bar <figure> (inline SVG, 340 wide) for the lesson's c_opcode (`0 := 10, [1:3] :/ 70, [8:F] :/ 20`). Segments: 0 = 10%; 1, 2 and 3 at about 23.3% each; 8 to F at 2.5% each (eight thin segments under one label); and a separate hatched box beside the bar, '4–7: not listed, never'. The caption gives the total weight, 100, and cites §18.5.3. Then the prompt 'Predict: if c_opcode used `[4'h1:4'h3] := 70` instead, how often is opcode 0?', followed by a <details> reveal holding a second bar row: total 10 + 210 + 20 = 240, so 0 ≈ 4.2%, each of 1..3 ≈ 29.2% and each of 8..F ≈ 1.0%. Arithmetic checked: 10/240, 70/240 and (20/8)/240. Verified against §18.5.3: ':= … range_weight = range_size × specified_weight'; ':/ … the weight for the entire range is the specified weight'; 'values not specified by the distribution and values specified with a total weight of zero … shall be treated as a constraint'.
additions.why: This is spine misconception 2 (:= and :/ are the same for ranges), checked on the page's real constraint. The bar makes 'dist also closes unlisted values' visible, and the counterfactual row puts the := trap right next to the correct reading.

additions.where: ### Reading dist weights, before the paragraph 'These numbers hold when no other constraint involves opcode' (line 266)
additions.what: Move the to-do item 'dist := vs :/. Flip the operator, then add c_big and see a dist membership conflict.' here word for word, then embed `<ConstraintSolverHeatmapVisualizer initialScenario="dist" scenarios={["dist"]} />`. The scenario's model is `x dist { 0 := 4, [1:3] := 4 }` with toggles c_not0 (x != 0) and c_big (x > 3). The learner predicts P(x == 0) = 25% with := and 50% with :/, then sees c_not0 keep the 1:1:1 ratio and c_big fail (only 0..3 are listed). Line 266 already refers to 'the heatmap's c_not0 toggle', so it now sits next to it.
additions.why: After the picture comes the experiment: the learner flips := and :/ and watches a membership conflict cause a failure, right where the rule is taught, instead of on a heatmap 150 lines earlier.

additions.where: ### solve…before changes the odds, never the legal set, after its second paragraph (line 272)
additions.what: A may / may-not recall table, 'What solve a before b can and cannot do', with columns Question, Answer and Clause (all §18.5.9). Changes the odds? Yes: a is drawn first, uniformly over its values that appear in some legal combination. Changes which combinations are legal? No. Can it make randomize() fail? No. Can it fix a failure? No, because the legal set is unchanged. Allowed on randc? No: randc is always solved first. A circular order (a before b, b before a)? Illegal. An array size? Yes, written data.size. Verified: §18.5.9 'does not change the solution space and, therefore, cannot cause the solver to fail', plus the restriction list (rand only, no randc, no circular dependencies, array.size allowed). Link the constraint-blocks sub-page, which has the experiment (ConstraintSolverExplorer initialMode="order"), so this page does not embed it again.
additions.why: This breaks the 640-word stretch with a one-glance answer to misconception 3. The section has no picture of its own, and the sub-page already holds the interactive.

additions.where: ### soft: a default with a rank, after the paragraph ending 'without editing the item' (line 284)
additions.what: A 'soft priority ladder' <ArchitectureDiagram> (cellWidth={120} gapX={48}), four generic nodes stacked in one column. Top: 'hard constraints', sublabel 'class or inline: always kept', state active. Then 'inline soft' (randomize() with {…}), 'derived-class soft' and 'base-class soft'. Causal edges between rungs are labelled 'beats' (5 characters, so no label-hides-edge warning). A badge or sublabel on each soft rung reads 'dropped whole, only on conflict'. Caption: '§18.5.13.1: inline beats the class, derived beats base, and within one block or class a later soft constraint beats an earlier one. The full list (external blocks, contained objects, foreach) is the table on the constraint-blocks page.' Give it the same name and shape as the ladder planned for constraint-blocks, so both pages and I-SV-2B can say 'the priority ladder'. Verified against §18.5.13.1. Optional if constraint-blocks ships its full ladder first; then link to it instead.
additions.why: The three priority rules are a numbered list with no picture. A ladder is the image learners reuse when a test layer's default does not win.

additions.where: ### soft: a default with a rank, after the ladder and before '**Predict before you read on:**' (line 286)
additions.what: Move the to-do item 'soft priority. A lone soft constraint holds on every call, not usually.' here word for word, then embed `<ConstraintSolverHeatmapVisualizer initialScenario="soft" scenarios={["soft"]} />`. Its model is c_def soft x == 0, a hard c_range x inside {[2:7]}, a later soft c_late x == 5, and an inline toggle `randomize() with { x > 3; }`. The learner predicts P(x == 0) = 100% alone, 0 with c_range (the hard rule wins), x = 5 with c_late (later wins) and 0 with the inline with (hard inline wins). The constraint-blocks sub-page uses ConstraintSolverExplorer initialMode="soft", a different component, so this is not a duplicate.

Caption: the size is decided first and is a state variable inside foreach (§18.5.7.1); which other variables join that step is tool-dependent; without a size constraint the array is not resized (§18.4: 'shall not be resized'), so a foreach on an empty array creates no constraints and the call still returns 1.
additions.why: The three size rules are the page's core array mechanism, and the 'no resize' rule (the debug challenge and quiz) has no picture today. The two dividers show both branches side by side.

additions.where: ### Guards: after 'Trace the list above and three variants' (L319), before the trace table (L321)
additions.what: P2. An InterviewQuestionPlayground titled 'Predict: a guard that reads through null'. Question: on n3 (next == null), what does `if (next.v > 3) v == 0;` do? Options and feedback. (a) 'No constraint: the guard is false.' Wrong: reading through null is ERROR, not FALSE (§18.5.12). (b) 'An evaluation error, so randomize() fails.' Correct: the guard itself reads through null, and an ERROR result fails the call (§18.5.12). (c) 'v == 0 is applied.' Wrong: nothing reads next.v as 0. (d) 'A conditional constraint, because next.v is random.' Wrong: n3 has no next object, so there is nothing random to read. The trace table that follows is the debrief.

additions.where: ### Guards: after the paragraph on part order and && / || (L330), before '**The key distinction.**' (L332)
additions.what: P1. A recall aid in the site's own layout, checked cell by cell against Figure 18-3. Table columns: joined with | strongest result → weakest | what it means for a null check. Rows: `&&` | FALSE → ERROR → RANDOM → TRUE | a FALSE null test outranks the ERROR beside it, so `next != null && next.v > 3` is safe. `\|\|` | TRUE → ERROR → RANDOM → FALSE | a TRUE part outranks an ERROR. `!` | swaps TRUE and FALSE; ERROR and RANDOM stay. Below it, a one-row strip 'final value → what the solver gets': TRUE → an unconditional constraint; FALSE → eliminated, no error; RANDOM → a conditional constraint; ERROR → an error, randomize() fails (§18.5.12). Escape || as \|\| inside markdown table cells.
additions.why: The four-valued guard logic is the hardest rule on the page and currently lives in two prose sentences. The dominance order compresses the 16-cell tables into two lines a learner can recall when writing guards.

additions.where: ### Guards: the '**The key distinction.**' paragraph (L332)

newComponentRequests: ImplicitSolveOrderExplorer: a deterministic, exactly enumerating lab for the three LRM solve orders, shareable with solver-debug.mdx and the I-SV-2B hub, whose audits ask for the same staged-solve picture. Presets: 'size-first' (ramp_item: len 1..10, d.size() == len, d[i] == i*30 on 8-bit elements; len = 10 is a dead end, 1 call in 10 fails); 'function-arg' (ones_item: 10-bit v, length == count_ones(v), length in 8..10; 56 of 1,024 succeed) and the §18.5.11 staged_item (y in {2, 4, 8}, x > limit(y), x < 6; y = 8 fails, 1 in 3); 'randc-first' (a small randc example). It draws the stage-1 choices as a tree with dead-end leaves (error tone, ✕) and the per-call failure probability. The learner predicts the failure rate, then toggles the fix (bound the size in its own constraint; rewrite as an expression) and the contrast (solve…before: same legal set, only the odds move). Clauses: §18.3, §18.4.2, §18.5.7.1, §18.5.11, §18.5.9.

ConstraintGuardEvaluator: a four-valued guard lab per §18.5.12 / Figure 18-3 on the n1 → n2 → n3 → null list. Presets: `if (next != null) v < next.v`; the unguarded `v < next.v`; `if (v > 10 && next != null) v < next.v`; `if (next.v > 3) v == 0`; `if (next != null && next.v > 3) v == 0`; `if (next == null || next.v > 3) v == 0` (on n3: TRUE || ERROR = TRUE, an unconditional v == 0); and the LRM's Example 1 `(x < y || a.x > b.x || a.x == 5) -> x+y == 10` with null toggles for a and b. It shows each subexpression's value (FALSE/TRUE/ERROR/RANDOM with glyphs, not colour only) on an expression tree, then the outcome: unconditional, eliminated, conditional, or an error that fails randomize(). Each node gets a gated prediction.

ConstraintSolverHeatmapVisualizer extension: add an 'if-else' scenario (a dangling vs a braced else over the 64 (x, y) pairs, with a toggle that moves the braces) and a 'unique' scenario (`unique {x, y}` removes the diagonal, P(x == 0) stays 1/8, plus a block that leaves too few values so the call fails). This page would then have interactive versions of its two remaining static solution-space pictures (the dangling-else table and the unique diagonal grid), on the exact-enumeration model it already uses.

ConstraintSolverExplorer: a `modes` prop to restrict the visible tabs. This page has to tell learners to 'stay on the Array size tab' because the dist, soft, order and hole tabs belong to I-SV-2A and solver-debug.

newComponentRequests: RandomizeControlPanel (high): a model-backed panel on a reduced-width bus_item (addr[3:0], len[3:0], non-rand err, knob max_len; the reduced widths are labelled) with code generated from model data. Each rand line has a rand_mode switch and each constraint block a constraint_mode switch. A call-form picker offers randomize(), randomize() with {addr[1:0] != 0}, randomize(len), randomize(err) and randomize(null), and current values are editable. Live bins show 'Random this call' versus 'State (value held)' and 'Active blocks' versus 'Off'. The learner predicts success and which fields may change; the reveal shows the legal values per field, the conflicting clauses on failure, and 'values kept, post_randomize() not called' (§18.6.3). Compile-error checks: rand_mode on a non-rand member (§18.8), an unknown block name (§18.9), the query form on a whole unpacked array (§18.8). Presets: 'bus_item'; 'ca' (the §18.11 CA class, including x = 127 so that randomize(v, w) fails because byte is signed); 'checker' (c_legal_* and c_shape_* blocks; a soft block reveals 'not specified, tool-dependent'). Debug mode has three seeded bugs (a frozen illegal value, a leaked constraint_mode, a same-name override), each with a HintLadder. It can reuse solve() from the constraint-solver model, with a thin adapter src/lib/randomize-control-model.ts.

RandomizeHookTimeline (high): two consecutive frame.randomize() calls drawn as beats (pre_randomize, solve, assign, post_randomize, return). The learner drops a statement card into pre or post of call 1 (max_len = 8; len = 4; len = 200; chk = payload.xor()). Toggles: 'call 1 fails (with {len == 0})' and an err_frame post_randomize() override with or without super. The learner predicts which call first sees the change, whether the item stays legal, and n_pre, n_post and chk; What and Why narration per beat (§18.6.2, §18.6.3). The card 'constraint_mode(0) inside pre_randomize()' must reveal 'not specified by IEEE 1800-2023; call it before randomize()' rather than an invented outcome.

ConstraintInheritanceMerger (high): the base bus_item block list (c_align, c_len, c_err) beside a derived-class editor whose block names are either an inherited name or a new one, with preset bodies (addr[1:0] != 0, len <= 4, len > 100). A handle-type and object-type picker sits below. The learner predicts the active set and the result of h.randomize() (succeeds or fails, and the legal len range); the reveal tags each block inherited, replaced or added and shows the solve (§18.5.2, randomize() is virtual). Under 'Show advanced', specifier toggles produce exactly the §18.5.2 errors (:extends with no base, :initial on an override, overriding a :final block, both :initial and :extends), a specifier on a static constraint (§18.5.10), and an unimplemented pure constraint in a non-abstract class. Copy PolymorphismDispatchVisualizer's handle-type and object-type picker pattern.

ModeStateTimeline (medium): a step-through with a scrubber over a statement script acting on objects a and b and a copy c = new a. Each object is a card with on/off switches (text labels plus a ▲ glyph when a switch changes). A static block or static rand variable is one switch on the class card, wired to every instance. At each '?' step the learner predicts a query result, whether the next randomize() succeeds, or which value category disappears. Presets: 'static vs ordinary block' (§18.5.10, §18.8), 'forgotten restore leaks into test B' (Tables 18-3 and 18-4), 'shallow copy carries the switches' (§8.12).

The analogy describes a picture (a roll of tickets torn off in order) that the page never draws.

Covers a signed int with only an upper bound (§6.11.3), an unqualified randomize() inside a class (§18.11), unchecked calls and assert() (§13.4.1, §20.11), a failed call keeping the old values (§18.6.3, §18.12), and when body() should use std::randomize(). Nothing shows the lopsided signed legal range, which is a spine misconception.

Covers the LRM 3/1/4 example, expression and zero weights, the all-zero case, narrow-width weights and randcase in a virtual sequence. Then six vocabulary bullets (production, production list, |, :=, terminal, nonterminal) come before the code they describe.

This is the lesson's main mental model, and it is all prose and numbered lists.

Lines 328-348 (about 430 words around the small methods table at lines 339-344). Covers why rows 4 and 5 shift b, the shared-object and shallow-copy cases (§8.12), 'the rule to carry', the process::self() note, and the caveat that a self-seeded object's new() still takes a draw. These are the subtle cases, and none of them has a picture.
Lines 414-432 (about 300 words, borderline: In a real testbench, the Recap bullets and the Make It Work intro). The page has no VisualRecap at all, so it has no one-glance summary picture.

It draws each process's and object's RNG as a 'ticket roll' (the lesson's anchor picture) with the seeding tree beside the code rows. The learner picks one edit: rerun; x = new() before a or after b; junk = $urandom, std::randomize(), randcase or randsequence between a and s; an extra a.randomize(); swapping two existing processes; s self-seeding on or off. additions.what:
Add a 'Where RNDFLD is reported' ArchitectureDiagram.

- **Routing nodes:**
  - 'seq body()' (kind sequence, sublabel '`uvm_do_with → `uvm_rand_send');
  - 'uvm_get_report_object()' (generic);
  - 'sqr' (kind sequencer, sublabel 'its m_rh handles RNDFLD', state active).
- **Fallback:** a dim 'uvm_root' node on an edge labelled 'if null'.
- **Three override nodes:**
  - 'sqr.set_report_severity_id_override' (ok, 'takes effect');
  - 'override on the test' (kind test, state error, 'no effect: wrong handler');
  - '+uvm_set_severity=*,RNDFLD,…' (ok, 'applied in each component's new()').

The caption cites the uvm-core 2020.3.1 sources:

- seq/uvm_sequence_item.svh: uvm_get_report_object() returns m_sequencer, or uvm_root when it is null, and uvm_process_report_message sends the message to l_report_object.m_rh.

findings: S2 line 573 - The heading of VisualRecap panel 3, "③ Size first, solve…before: odds only" (with "✓ same 4 legal cells, new odds" at line 586), groups the language's size-before-elements order with solve…before as an odds-only change. IEEE 1800-2023 §18.5.7.1 says this implicit size/iterative ordering "can cause the solver to fail in some situations". The page's own Push Further table (line 815, 'Array sizes before foreach and reduction constraints … Yes, in some situations') and line 807 say the same thing. So the summary card that learners are told to memorise teaches the opposite of the rule. -> Retitle the panel to "③ solve…before: odds only". If size-first should stay on the card, give it a separate line such as "size first: odds here, but it can fail with foreach (§18.5.7.1)". Optionally say 'Sizes are solved before elements (§18.4); with foreach this order can fail (§18.5.7.1)' in the rule prop too.

S3 lines 576-584 - The panel 3 bars are not to scale. The joint row totals 4×12 = 48 and the ordered row totals 28 + 3×5 = 43. A 28:5 ratio cannot come from solve…before: over four legal cells with one tall and three equal, the only possible split is 1/2 against 1/6 each, which is 3:1. -> Make the ordered bars 24 tall and 8 tall (total 48). The joint bars stay at 12.

S3 line 327 - The SequenceDiagram note 'no resize: data keeps its current size' uses tone "error", but this is legal, defined behaviour (§18.4: the array is not resized and its existing elements are randomized). The error tone suggests a failure. -> Use tone "normal" or "active" and leave the warning to the caption ("a fresh packet's empty data stays empty").

S3 line 741 - 'disable soft changes the result only where the earlier default does not conflict with the later one' overgeneralises. Row 3 has no later block, and there disable soft does change the result (from 3 to unconstrained). -> Reword to 'Compare rows 1-2 with rows 4-5: when a later soft constraint exists, disable soft changes the result only where the earlier default does not conflict with it.'
